newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh's lawyer suggests foreign help in bombing.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh's lawyer suggests foreign help in bombing.

text.p: People with links in Germany and the Middle East also wanted to blow up the Oklahoma City building for which Timothy McVeigh was sentenced to death last week, his attorney, Stephen Jones, said on the CBS programme "60 minutes" on Sunday.
Jones said that information reached the U.S. government through a paid and trusted informant who passed lie-detector tests.

He said witnesses saw sniffing dogs and bomb disposal trucks in the federal complex in Oklahoma City in the hours before the bombing, in which 168 people died, and theorised that local law enforcement could not now admit they knew about a threat after the explosion.
A former Army buddy of McVeigh's, Terry Nichols, also faces charges in the bombing and is to be tried later.

In the interview, Jones said there was evidence to suggest that McVeigh "may simply have been a patsy; that he may have been used and involved by others as... sort of a convenient fall guy and permitted himself to be used....".

"I know that others had an interest in blowing up the Murrah building several years ago," Murrah told "60 Minutes". "... I know that they were told to prepare. I know they had copies of homemade C4 (plastic explosive) books; they had bunkers. I know they had connections in Germany. I know the people there had connections within Germany, had connections in the Middle East."
"I know who some of these people are," Jones continued. "I know that their leader told them, 'You know what needs to be done, so now go do it.'"

"I know this information came to the federal government through an informant, regularly polygraphed, who passed them (the lie detector tests); who was paid several thousand dollars for this information and was determined to be reliable and credible," Jones told CBS.

"I know that there are people that swear that on the morning of April the 19th, they saw sniffing dogs in the federal complex in downtown Oklahoma City, and very nearby, bomb disposal trucks from the Oklahoma County Sheriff's Office. That suggests to me that the government had some information that indicated that the federal buildings in Oklahoma City could be at risk.... And then, when the building blew up, they could not ever admit that they know," Jones said, describing that scenario as a theory.
In other comments, Jones told CBS:
-- He planned to challenge the verdict with a motion for a new trial and an appeal.
-- It could take four years to execute McVeigh if all the appeals failed.
-- If the jury was correct, McVeigh "did a great wrong" but he did not consider his client evil.
-- He could not discuss what he knew about the case further and he had no idea whether McVeigh would ever talk about the bombing.
